project.name: Anstruther

properties.ACCURACY: Digitised from designation map based on OS Mapping.  See COMPILER's maps for details.

project.boundarySource: Historic Environment Scotland ANSTRUTHER Conservation Area, buffered 300m for settlement study
project.researchNotes: Sequential place 5 of 14. Strict settlement merit, See, café-led Eat, all named trail providers, picnic, public visitor parking, public toilets, access, transport, dogs and complete local HES/NRHE construction dates were checked before continuing. The Cellar, Dreel Tavern, fish bar, Wee Chippy and Waterfront are excluded from Eat because they are primarily restaurant, pub or takeaway offers. Cellardyke remains separately audited.

touristAppeal.label: Exceptional Destination
touristAppeal.summary: Anstruther remains a top-tier coastal destination, centred on its harbour, Scottish Fisheries Museum, Reaper, Isle of May trips, town trails and broad daytime café offer. Meal-led restaurants and takeaways are no longer shown as Eat.
touristAppeal.dogAccessSummary: The harbour, town trail, coast path, Treasure Trail and several excellent Eats work well with a dog, but the two flagship paid experiences do not: the ferry explicitly carries no dogs and the museum only confirms assistance dogs. That materially reduces, but does not erase, the town’s value for dog owners.

visitorHighlights.name: Scottish Fisheries Museum
visitorHighlights.reason: A national museum with substantial galleries, historic buildings, a working boatyard and preserved vessels.
visitorHighlights.openingTimes: Mon–Sat 10:00–16:30; Sun 11:00–16:30. Closed Tuesdays November–March. Last entry 15:30.

editorialReview.scoreRationale: National significance, deep collections and unusually strong harbour setting with clear current visit information.

visitorHighlights.name: Isle of May Ferry – May Princess
visitorHighlights.reason: A destination-scale wildlife voyage with meaningful island time, ranger welcome, cliff circuit and transparent 2026 booking information.
visitorHighlights.tagline: Land on the Isle of May
visitorHighlights.timeToSpend: 4½–5 hours landing trip; about 2¼ hours cruise-around
visitorHighlights.openingTimes: Seasonal sailings April–September; times vary with tide and weather. Advance booking strongly advised.
visitorHighlights.admission: Landing trip: adult £40, concession £35, child £20. Cruise-around: adult £30, concession £25, child £15.

editorialReview.scoreRationale: An exceptional seasonal wildlife and island-history experience, slightly reduced for weather dependence, seasonality and physical access constraints.

visitorHighlights.name: Anstruther Harbour and Waterfront
visitorHighlights.reason: A large and legible working waterfront where museum, ferry, fishing boats, leisure craft, historic piers and food all reinforce one another.
visitorHighlights.openingTimes: Open-air waterfront; daylight visit recommended. Respect working areas and harbour instructions.

editorialReview.scoreRationale: A strong, active waterfront with multiple linked visitor reasons, reduced because it is a working public harbour rather than a managed attraction.

townGuide.characterTag: National fishing museum and Isle of May harbour
townGuide.headline: The East Neuk’s most complete maritime day out
townGuide.intro: Anstruther remains a top-tier coastal destination, centred on its harbour, Scottish Fisheries Museum, Reaper, Isle of May trips, town trails and broad daytime café offer. Meal-led restaurants and takeaways are no longer shown as Eat.
perfectFor: Visitors wanting indoor depth and an outdoor waterfront

suggestedFirstVisit.title: Build the day around museum or ferry
suggestedFirstVisit.summary: Reserve the seasonal ferry first if it is your priority; otherwise start at the museum, circle the harbour, eat on Shore Street and finish with the town trail or a coast-path section.

dontMiss: Isle of May Ferry – May Princess
Anstruther – Old Castle & Harbour Treasure Trail
townGuide.suggestedTime: Half day without the ferry; a full day with an Isle of May landing
townGuide.visitorMood: A genuinely complete destination rather than a single-view stop: deep maritime interpretation, a major wildlife excursion, strong food and useful facilities all fit within a compact walkable centre.

features.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
features.fullDescription: William Williamson, 1901. Single storey, 9-bay, broadly T-plan school building with symmetrical gables and Art Nouveau influences. (1955 addition to the west elevation by Fife County Architects is not considered of special interest in listing terms at the time of review). Slightly advanced 3-bay gable to centre, flanked by dormer windows with pointed-arch pediments breaking eaves at 2nd and 8th bays. Squared and snecked sandstone rubble with ashlar dressings and ashlar base course. Carved thistle motifs to gables and dormers. Timber roof lantern with slightly battered angles, classical hoodmoulds, ogee-cap and metal weathervane finial. Rounded and corbelled corner angles to rear. Rounded pediments to dormers breaking eaves to rear. Slightly swept pitch to piended roofs. Predominantly multi-pane glazing in timber sash and case frames. Cast iron rainwater goods. Grey slates. There is a sloping grassed bank to the front of the building with a stepped retaining wall with chamfered copes.

features.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
features.fullDescription: David Henry, 1884-86, school and adjoining school masters house; J Currie, 1909, library/hall addition to rear. Single storey, 7-bay, roughly I-plan school building with advanced gabled outer bays and advanced, square-plan, 3-stage tower to centre in the collegiate Gothic manner. (1930s classroom block by George Sandilands and all 1956 additions by Fife County Architects to the north are not considered of special interest in listing terms at the time of review). Squared and snecked sandstone rubble with ashlar dressings. Base course and moulded eaves course. Mullioned windows. Four-centred arch above main entrance with carved tympanum by John Rhind depicting a ship leaving a castellated harbour. Doorpiece is flanked by buttresses. Tower above has shallow-pointed, louvred openings at third stage and a castellated parapet. Former library/hall adjoining to rear has single storey wings flanking a slightly advanced gable (east elevation) with three tall round-headed windows and shouldered skews. Predominantly multi-pane glazing in timber sash and case frames. Grey slates, pitched roof. Red clay cresting to ridges. Corniced ridge and end stacks to side and rear elevations. The interior was seen in 2015. Largely typical of buildings for education of its date, with various later remodelling of spaces and fixtures and fittings to accommodate the changing needs of the school over time. The 1909 assembly hall was reconfigured to form a library during the 1956 remodelling and extension to the school. It retains a well-detailed early 20th century double-height, top-lit, trussed timber ceiling.

features.name: 11 Rodger Street, Cellardyke
alternativeNames: CELLARDYKE, RODGER STREET, NOS 1A, 1-9 (INCLUSIVE), 11-35 (ODD NOS), INCLUDING ANCILLARY BUILDINGS AND BOUNDARY WALLS
features.shortDescription: CELLARDYKE, RODGER STREET, NOS 1A, 1-9 (INCLUSIVE), 11-35 (ODD NOS), INCLUDING ANCILLARY BUILDINGS AND BOUNDARY WALLS
features.fullDescription: Begun by Thomas Brown, builder, 1877. 2-storey and attic paired (excepting No 1) 2-bay terraced tenements purpose-built for local fishing community with single and 2-storey freestanding fishing gear storage to rear terminating in corner shop at N (No 35). Coursed tooled sandstone to street elevation, rubble to rear and sides, excepting N elevation of No 35 which has squared and snecked tooled sandstone. Rectangular piended stair projections to rear, margined window and door openings, polygonal piended dormers, pairs of houses stepped at roofline. Some minor alterations and additions. E (PRINCIPAL) ELEVATION: to left, No 1, 3-bay 2-storey and attic terraced house, to right 10 paired 2-storey and attic terraced tenements, to far right corner shop with chamfered margins. Slight variations to the properties, especially window openings, including bipartite ground floor window to No 6. Variety of glazing, some 12-pane and 4-pane (those to No 35 with horns) timber sash and case windows, some modern. Modern rooflights. Grey slates. Large gable end stacks and ridge stacks at division of paired tenements. Various door types, some timber 4-panel, some modern, simple rectangular fanlights above. INTERIOR: No 3, modernised. ANCILLARY BUILDINGS: to W, 2-storey 2-bay predominantly terraced rubble-built fishing gear storage sheds forming courtyard with tenements, some with forestairs to W elevation. Few loft hatches to E elevation extant, that to No 3 remains. Variety of glazing, some 6-pane fixed lights. Some simple timber boarded doors. Some ridge stacks remain. Broadly, pantiles to S, slates to N. BOUNDARY WALLS: low rubble walls to E elevation with predominantly flat coping. High dividing walls forming sides of rear courtyards of properties.

features.name: 22 Rodger Street, Cellardyke
alternativeNames: CELLARDYKE, RODGER STREET, NOS 10, 14-38 (EVEN NOS), INCLUDING BOUNDARY WALLS AND ANCILLARY BUILDINGS
features.shortDescription: CELLARDYKE, RODGER STREET, NOS 10, 14-38 (EVEN NOS), INCLUDING BOUNDARY WALLS AND ANCILLARY BUILDINGS
features.fullDescription: Begun by Robert Williamson, builder and plasterer, 1878. No 38 with 1883 datestone. 2-storey and attic paired 2-bay terraced tenements purpose-built for local fishing community with predominantly single storey freestanding fishing gear storage to rear terminating in corner shop at N (No 38). Coursed tooled sandstone to street elevation, rubble to rear and S elevation, squared and snecked tooled sandstone to N elevation. Base course, rectangular piended stair projections to rear, chamfered window and door openings, few remaining cast-iron brackets supporting guttering, polygonal piended dormers (crowstepped dormerheads to No 38) to W elevation, variety of dormers to E elevation, pairs of houses stepped at roofline. Some minor alterations and additions. W (PRINCIPAL) ELEVATION: 7 paired 2-storey and attic terraced tenements, that to N with corner shop (No 38). To S paired bipartite ground floor windows to No 10. Nos 20, 22 and 24 have some decorative cast-iron gutter brackets remaining. Variety of glazing, some 4-pane timber sash and case windows with horns, some modern. Modern rooflights. Grey slates. Large gable end stacks and ridge stacks at division of paired properties. Various door types, some timber 4-panel, some modern, simple rectangular fanlights above. INTERIOR: No 10, modernised. No 22, ground floor sitting room with tiled cast-iron fireplace with inset cupboard to left, glazed above. No. 14 (former home of Robert Wiilliamson) with an unusual and high-quality plastered ceiling (restored in 2019), including cornicing, a large, very ornate ceiling rose, and roundels with cherub-type figures. ANCILLARY BUILDINGS: predominantly single storey terraced fishing gear storage sheds forming courtyard to rear with tenements. Pantiled. Simple timber boarded doors. Some surviving gable stacks. BOUNDARY WALLS: low coursed sandstone walls to W with predominantly chamfered coping. High dividing walls forming sides of rear courtyards of properties.

sources.limitations: The spatial index provides a representative site point, names and classifications. It does not establish construction dates; detailed source records require individual review.

sources.name: Historic Environment Scotland Scheduled Monuments spatial data
sources.coverage: Scheduled monuments intersecting the strict editorial boundary
sources.accessMethod: Developer-supplied local HES Shapefile; exact boundary intersection
sources.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
sources.limitations: The spatial layer supplies designation and location, not a historic construction period. Undated records remain in the catalogue but are hidden from the heat map.

sources.name: Historic Environment Scotland Listed Buildings spatial data
sources.coverage: Anstruther editorial district plus 500m heritage buffer; buffer records are retained as related context
sources.accessMethod: Developer-supplied local HES Shapefile; exact polygon selection
sources.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; retain Historic Environment Scotland attribution.
sources.limitations: Anstruther has no separate NRS locality boundary. The transparent visitor-guide editorial boundary is used and buffer records remain context only. The source supplies statutory designation and location metadata, not construction dates.

sources.name: OpenStreetMap current community places
sources.coverage: Food and drink, picnic/rest, art, memorial, historic, leisure, visitor, amenity, parking and natural-sight places within the Anstruther study area plus its 300m buffer.
sources.accessMethod: Read-only Overpass API query, then exact point-in-study-area filtering and source-ID/name-proximity deduplication.
sources.licence: Open Database Licence (ODbL) v1.0; © OpenStreetMap contributors.
sources.limitations: Current voluntary mapping only. Tags, names and locations may change; this optional icon layer is excluded from historic evidence, dates, heat scoring, totals and historic exports.

sources.name: Historic Environment Scotland Conservation Areas spatial data
sources.limitations: A conservation area is a historic-core study boundary, not an administrative settlement boundary.
